title: Non-Alignment: Aims and Achievements

cards.h: A third way in a two-camp world
cards.b:
When the Cold War divided the globe into two blocs, a group of newly independent states said: we will not join either. That was the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM).

It is one of the most important Indian contributions to world politics. Jawaharlal Nehru was its architect, along with Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah. UPSC returns to it often: its aims, achievements, failures and relevance today.

Do not mix up three words:

  • Non-alignment: independent judgement on each issue, with no military bloc membership.
  • Neutrality: staying out of a particular war, a legal status.
  • Isolationism: staying out of world affairs altogether.

India was never neutral or isolated. It spoke on Korea, Suez, Hungary, Vietnam and disarmament. A frequent question is whether non-alignment is still useful. A good answer links it to today's "strategic autonomy" and "multi-alignment".

cards.h: Origins: Asia, decolonisation and the Bandung meeting
cards.b:
• 1947. Nehru convened the Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi, before independence. He wanted Asia to find its own voice.
  • 1954. The Colombo Powers (Burma, Ceylon, India, Indonesia, Pakistan) met. India and China signed the Panchsheel agreement on Tibet on 29 April 1954.
  • Bandung, 18-24 April 1955. The Asian-African Conference brought together 29 states. It condemned colonialism and racism and issued the ten-point Declaration on the Promotion of World Peace and Cooperation, which built on Panchsheel.

Panchsheel, the five principles

  1. Mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty.
  2. Mutual non-aggression.
  3. Non-interference in internal affairs.
  4. Equality and mutual benefit.
  5. Peaceful coexistence.

Bandung was not yet NAM but it created the mood. China's Zhou Enlai attended, and the US and USSR were not invited.

The founding summit was held in Belgrade, 1-6 September 1961, with 25 member states. The "big five" leaders were Nehru (India), Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Nkrumah (Ghana).

A preparatory meeting in Cairo (June 1961) fixed the criteria for membership. They included: an independent policy based on peaceful coexistence and non-alignment; support for national independence movements; no membership of a multilateral military alliance linked to great-power conflict; and no bilateral military pact with a great power.

Core aims

  • End colonialism, racism and apartheid.
  • Peaceful settlement of disputes and general disarmament.
  • Respect for sovereignty and equality of states.
  • Economic development, and a fairer economic order.
  • Reform of the UN.

Nehru spoke of avoiding the "war of the blocs" and widening the "area of peace". Nehru's own thinking is in The Discovery of India (1946) and in his speeches collected as India's Foreign Policy.

The movement grew from 25 members in 1961 to about 120 today, which makes it the largest group of states outside the UN itself. It has no secretariat or permanent headquarters; a rotating chair coordinates it.

India hosted the 7th summit in March 1983, and Indira Gandhi chaired the movement until 1986. The 18th summit was in Baku (2019) and the 19th in Kampala, Uganda (January 2024).

• Independence of judgement. India would decide each issue on its merits, not on a bloc line.
  • Anti-colonialism and anti-racism. This was a moral and strategic aim from India's own experience.
  • Peace for development. A newly independent poor country needed peace, trade and technology from both sides.
  • Reduce the Cold War. Nehru believed that alliances spread tension. He opposed SEATO and the Baghdad Pact.
  • Strategic autonomy. Keep freedom to act, with the ability to take aid from the US, the USSR and others.

It was both principle and interest. Realist critics call it a prudent policy for a weak state to extract gains from both sides. Idealist readers call it a moral stance for peace.

Nehru's phrase was a "policy of non-alignment", not neutrality. He also said that where freedom or justice is threatened, India cannot be neutral.

• Decolonisation. It gave newly independent states a voice and pushed the UN toward the 1960 Declaration on Granting Independence to Colonial Countries.
  • Anti-apartheid and Namibia. NAM kept pressure on South Africa and supported liberation movements.
  • Reduced bloc pressure. Members like India, Egypt and Yugoslavia could take help from both camps, and avoid being satellites.
  • Economic agenda. The Algiers summit (1973) called for a New International Economic Order. The UN General Assembly's Sixth Special Session adopted the NIEO Declaration in May 1974. NAM worked with the G-77 (1964) and UNCTAD.
  • Disarmament. NAM backed the Partial Test Ban Treaty, the NPT debates and disarmament conferences.
  • Palestine. Consistent support for Palestinian rights.
  • Mediation. In Korea, Indo-China and the Suez crisis, non-aligned diplomacy helped to keep talks open.

It also strengthened the idea that small states have a voice in the UN, which is why the UN's membership expansion mattered.

• Internal divisions. Members quarrelled with each other: India and China (1962), India and Pakistan, Iran and Iraq (1980-88). The Egypt-Israel peace treaty of 1979 caused rifts among Arab members.
  • Tilt towards Moscow? Cuba's Fidel Castro, at Havana in 1979, argued that the Soviet bloc was the "natural ally" of the movement. India's 1971 treaty with the USSR and its soft response on Afghanistan (1979) drew the same charge.
  • Weak institutions. No secretariat, no enforcement, decisions by consensus.
  • Hard security gap. Non-alignment did not save India in 1962.
  • Economic weakness. The NIEO call was largely resisted by the North. The 1980s debt crisis divided the South.
  • After 1991. With one bloc gone, critics said NAM lost its reason: "non-aligned with whom?" Many members were drifting into alliances.

Defenders reply that NAM still has work: equity in global governance, UN reform, climate justice and freedom from great-power rivalry.

Why it still matters

  • The principles (sovereignty, peaceful settlement, anti-colonialism) are timeless.
  • A new US-China rivalry and the Ukraine war push many Global South states to avoid choosing sides.
  • It supports a voice for developing countries on debt, climate and trade.

Why it has faded

  • No bipolar structure to stand apart from.
  • Divergent interests of 120 members.
  • India's leaders have preferred forums such as the G20, BRICS, the SCO and the Quad, rather than NAM summits.

The 2012 report Nonalignment 2.0, by a group of Indian strategists (published by the Centre for Policy Research), argued India should keep strategic autonomy, but with a new, more flexible approach: engage all powers, build capabilities, and avoid being tied to any one.

• Cold War. India took Soviet help on steel, defence and Kashmir diplomacy, and American food aid and loans. The 1971 treaty was framed as a response to a "Washington-Beijing-Islamabad" axis.
  • 1990s. After the Soviet collapse, India reached out to the US, Israel, ASEAN (Look East, 1992) and the EU.
  • Today's phrases. Strategic autonomy, multi-alignment (a term used by Shashi Tharoor and others) and Vishwa Bandhu. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar's The India Way (2020) explains the approach of engaging many poles at once.
  • Practice. India sits in the Quad with the US, Japan and Australia, but also in BRICS and the SCO with Russia and China. It buys Russian oil and arms, and builds defence ties with the US and France.
  • Global South voice. The "Voice of Global South Summit" (2023), the African Union's G20 membership under India's presidency, and India's BRICS chair in 2026.

Critics say multi-alignment is hedging without a firm anchor. Supporters say it fits a multipolar world.

"Non-alignment was a policy of the Cold War, with no place in a post-Cold War world." Comment.
"Assess the achievements and failures of the Non-Aligned Movement."

Structure: define and separate from neutrality. Origins: Asian Relations Conference 1947, Panchsheel 1954, Bandung 1955, Belgrade 1961. Aims. Achievements (decolonisation, NIEO, disarmament). Failures (divisions, 1962, 1971 treaty criticism, no institutions). Then relevance: Nonalignment 2.0, strategic autonomy, Quad plus BRICS.

Keep a balanced verdict: the tool changed, the aim of autonomy remains.

quiz.q: The Bandung Conference was held in:
quiz.w: Bandung, Indonesia, 18-24 April 1955; 29 Asian and African states.

quiz.q: The first NAM summit took place in:
Which leader was NOT one of the five founders of NAM usually named?
quiz.w: The founders: Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno, Nkrumah.

quiz.q: The Panchsheel principles were first formally stated in the India-China agreement on:
quiz.w: The Agreement on Trade and Intercourse between the Tibet Region of China and India, April 1954.

quiz.q: India hosted the 7th NAM summit in:
quiz.w: New Delhi, March 1983, with Indira Gandhi as chair.

quiz.q: The Algiers NAM summit (1973) is linked to the call for:
quiz.w: The NIEO Declaration followed in 1974 at the UN.

quiz.q: Fidel Castro's 1979 Havana argument said NAM should:
o: Treat the Soviet bloc as its 'natural ally'
quiz.w: Many members, including India, rejected this.

quiz.q: Roughly how many members does NAM have today?
quiz.w: About 120 member states and several observers.

quiz.q: The report Nonalignment 2.0 (2012) was published by:
quiz.w: A group of Indian strategists associated with CPR.

quiz.q: Non-alignment differs from neutrality because it:
o: Means staying out of all wars
Allows independent judgement on each issue
quiz.w: Neutrality is a legal status in war; non-alignment is a policy of independence from blocs.
